name: Awesome Habits
tagline: A habit tracker with streaks, reminders and progress charts.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A habit tracker is a checkbox, a date, and a streak counter. There is no network, no proprietary data, and nothing an agent cannot model in an afternoon: habits table, completions table, a heatmap, a streak query. The paid version buys you taste, a real mobile app, and notifications that actually fire, which is not nothing but also not a moat. The one honest risk is behavioural: a tracker you built yourself is a tracker you feel free to abandon, and half of what you pay a habit app for is the sunk cost that keeps you opening it. Build it, keep it on your phone home screen, and see if you still care in three weeks.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you define habits, tap them done each day, and see streaks plus a year heatmap per habit.
requirements: Node 20+ and a place to run it (laptop, home server, or a cheap VPS)
A browser you can install a PWA into if you want it on your phone
Optional: HTTPS and a domain if you want phone access outside your network
whatYouLose: A polished native app with widgets and watch support
Push notifications and reminders that reliably fire on iOS
Cloud sync across devices without you running or paying for anything
Someone else's design taste on the charts and streak animations
Backups and data recovery you did not have to think about
moatNotes: The habit tracker category is thousands of near identical apps competing purely on feel and reminder reliability, which is exactly the kind of moat that evaporates when you only have to please yourself.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because habit apps are sold on momentum, not features. Once you have a two hundred day streak inside an app, that history is the product, and nobody wants to migrate a streak. People also pay for the parts that are genuinely annoying to self-host: a native app that opens instantly, a widget on the lock screen, and a reminder at 8pm that arrives even when your laptop is asleep. If you never open your DIY version, the four dollars a month was the better deal.
notes: The build is trivial; the habit is the hard part, and no amount of code fixes that.
prompt:
Build a single-user habit tracker I run myself. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript
- Tailwind CSS
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/habits.db, created and migrated on first boot
- No ORM, no auth library, no external APIs

Data model:
- habits: id, name, emoji, color, cadence ('daily' or 'weekly'), target_per_week (int, used when cadence is weekly), archived (bool), created_at
- completions: id, habit_id, date (YYYY-MM-DD, local time), UNIQUE(habit_id, date)

Screens:
1. Today: list of active habits as large tap targets, tap toggles today's completion (optimistic UI), shows current streak per habit.
2. Habit detail: 365 day heatmap grid, current streak, longest streak, completion rate over the last 30 days, and a way to backfill or remove any past date.
3. Manage: create, edit, reorder, archive habits. Archived habits keep their history and drop off Today.

Logic requirements:
- Streaks computed in SQL or plain TypeScript, no date libraries beyond date-fns if you want one.
- Weekly habits: a week counts as satisfied when completions in that ISO week reach target_per_week; streaks count weeks, not days.
- All dates are local, never UTC-shifted. Write a couple of tests for the streak function with vitest.

Also include:
- A PWA manifest and icons so I can install it on my phone home screen, offline shell only, no service worker sync games.
- GET /api/export returning all data as JSON, and a POST /api/import that restores it.
- A one line npm script that copies the SQLite file into ./backups with a timestamp.

Explicitly out of scope: reminders and push notifications, multi user, social features, gamification badges, AI anything.

Secrets, if any ever appear, go in .env and .env.example. Finish with a README that says how to run it, how to back it up, and how to expose it to my phone over Tailscale.
